facts: **18 chapters, 700 verses**, in the Bhīṣma Parva of the Mahābhārata (chapters 23–40). Each chapter is called a *yoga*: 2 Sāṃkhya, 3 Karma, 4 Jñāna-karma-saṃnyāsa, 6 Dhyāna (Ātma-saṃyama), 12 Bhakti, 13 Kṣetra-kṣetrajña, 14 Guṇatraya-vibhāga, 16 Daivāsura-sampad, 17 Śraddhātraya-vibhāga, 18 Mokṣa-saṃnyāsa.
Definitions of yoga: ***samatvaṃ yoga ucyate*** (2.48), ***yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam*** (2.50), ***duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyogaṃ yoga-saṃjñitam*** (6.23).
**Sthitaprajña** (steady wisdom) is described in 2.54–72; the downward chain from dwelling on objects to ruin — attachment, desire, anger, delusion, loss of memory, loss of buddhi — is 2.62–63.
**Karma yoga**: the right is to action alone, never to its fruits (2.47); act as yajña (3.9); fight *nirāśīḥ, nirmamaḥ, vigata-jvaraḥ* (3.30).

**Dhyāna yoga** (ch. 6): a clean, firm seat, neither too high nor too low, of kuśa grass, deer-skin and cloth (6.11); body, head and neck erect, gaze at the nose-tip (6.13); yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little (6.16–17); the mind is controlled by **abhyāsa and vairāgya** (6.35).

**Three guṇas** (ch. 14), and threefold faith, food, sacrifice, austerity and charity (ch. 17): sāttvika food is juicy, oily, nourishing (17.8); rājasika is bitter, sour, salty, very hot (17.9); tāmasika is stale and impure (17.10). Austerity of body, speech and mind: 17.14–16.
**Demonic qualities** (16.4): *dambha, darpa, abhimāna, krodha, pāruṣya, ajñāna*. The triple gate to hell: *kāma, krodha, lobha* (16.21).
Devotee dear to the Lord: *adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānāṃ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca* (12.13–20). Final teaching: *sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja* (18.66).

**Opening and close**: the first word is *dharma* (*dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre*, 1.1, spoken by Dhṛtarāṣṭra to Sañjaya); the last verse (18.78) is Sañjaya's *yatra yogeśvaraḥ kṛṣṇo*. **Speakers**: Kṛṣṇa ~574 verses, Arjuna ~84, Sañjaya ~41, Dhṛtarāṣṭra 1.

**Ch. 2.20** (the self is not born and does not die), 2.22 (worn-out clothes), **2.47** *karmaṇy evādhikāras te*, **4.7–8** *yadā yadā hi dharmasya… paritrāṇāya sādhūnām*, **18.66** *sarva-dharmān parityajya* — the most quoted verses.

**Ch. 3**: yajña cycle (3.14); *svadharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ* (3.35); the seats of desire are **the senses, mind and intellect** (3.40); the self is above the buddhi (3.42). **Ch. 4**: *jñāna-agni* burns all karma (4.37); nothing is as purifying as knowledge (4.38); *śraddhāvān labhate jñānam* (4.39).

**Ch. 5–6**: the yukta is *sama-darśin* (5.18); *uddhared ātmanātmānam* — the self is one's own friend and enemy (6.5); the mind is hard to control but held by **abhyāsa and vairāgya** (6.34–35); *yukta-āhāra-vihārasya* (6.17).

**Ch. 7**: Kṛṣṇa's eightfold prakṛti — **earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego** (7.4); **four kinds of devotees** — ārta, jijñāsu, arthārthī, jñānī, the jñānī is dearest (7.16–17). **Ch. 8**: *oṃ ity ekākṣaraṃ brahma* (8.13); uttarāyaṇa and dakṣiṇāyana paths (8.24–25).

**Ch. 12**: the bhakta's qualities (12.13–20), *adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānām*. **Ch. 13**: 20 qualities of knowledge beginning *amānitvam adambhitvam* (13.7–11). **Ch. 15**: the inverted **aśvattha** tree with roots above (15.1); **kṣara, akṣara and puruṣottama** (15.16–18).

**Ch. 16**: 26 divine qualities beginning ***abhayam*** (16.1–3); **three gates to hell — kāma, krodha, lobha** (16.21). **Ch. 18**: five causes of action — adhiṣṭhāna, kartā, karaṇa, ceṣṭā, daiva (18.14); sāttvika/rājasika/tāmasika knowledge, action, doer, buddhi, dhṛti and sukha (18.20–39).
traps: **Chapter names vs number** are asked often: 3 Karma, **4 Jñāna-karma-saṃnyāsa**, **5 Karma-saṃnyāsa**, 6 Dhyāna/Ātma-saṃyama, 7 Jñāna-vijñāna, 8 Akṣara-brahma, 9 Rāja-vidyā-rāja-guhya, 10 Vibhūti, 11 Viśvarūpa-darśana, 12 Bhakti, 15 Puruṣottama. Chapters 4 and 5 are the ones most often confused.
**Definitions of yoga**: *samatvaṃ* is 2.48, *karmasu kauśalam* 2.50, *duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyogaṃ* 6.23. Don't place *karmasu kauśalam* in ch. 3.
**Three gates to hell (16.21)**: kāma, krodha, lobha. **Seats of desire (3.40)**: indriyas, manas, buddhi. Both lists have three items.
**Sāttvika food** (17.8) is juicy, oily, nourishing and pleasing. **Bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and burning** foods are **rājasika** (17.9), not tāmasika.

facts: **Haṭha Pradīpikā (2.22)** has six karmas: *dhauti, basti, neti, trāṭaka, nauli, kapālabhāti*; they are needed only when fat or phlegm is in excess (2.21). Gajakaraṇī is added in 2.38. Nauli is called the crown of haṭha practices (2.34).
**Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā (1.12)**: *dhauti, vasti, neti, laulikī, trāṭaka, kapālabhāti*. Śodhana (purification) is the fruit of ṣaṭkarma (1.10).

Gheraṇḍa's **dhauti** has four kinds: **antar-dhauti** (vātasāra, vārisāra, vahnisāra/agnisāra — navel pressed to the spine **100 times** — and bahiṣkṛta), **danta-dhauti** (danta-mūla, jihvā-mūla, two karṇa-randhra, kapāla-randhra: five), **hṛd-dhauti** (daṇḍa, vamana, vāsa) and **mūla-śodhana**.
Gheraṇḍa's **basti**: jala-basti and śuṣka (dry) basti; **neti**: a thread through the nose; **kapālabhāti**: vātakrama, vyutkrama, śītkrama.
**Vastra-dhauti** cloth: four fingers wide, **15 hastas** long in Haṭha Pradīpikā (2.24); **20 hastas** in the Haṭharatnāvalī.
**Haṭharatnāvalī** has *aṣṭakarma*: cakri, nauli, dhauti, neti, basti, gajakaraṇī, trāṭaka, mastaka-bhrānti.

Typical benefits asked: dhauti cures cough, asthma, spleen disorders, leprosy and 20 kapha diseases (HP 2.25); trāṭaka cures eye diseases and gives clairvoyance (HP 2.32); kapālabhāti destroys kapha disorders (HP 2.35).

**HP order of the six** (2.22): dhauti, basti, neti, trāṭaka, **nauli (5th)**, kapālabhāti. HP 2.21: those with **excess fat or phlegm (medaḥ-śleṣmādhika)** should do the ṣaṭkarma first; others, whose doṣas are balanced, go straight to prāṇāyāma. HP 2.37: some teachers hold that prāṇāyāma alone dries up all impurities.

**HP trāṭaka**: gaze without blinking at a small point until tears come; destroys eye diseases and sloth, and is to be kept **secret like a golden casket** (2.31–32). **HP kapālabhāti**: inhale and exhale rapidly **like a blacksmith's bellows** (*bhastrāval lohakārasya*, 2.35).

**HP basti**: sit in navel-deep water in **utkaṭāsana**, insert a bamboo tube in the anus and draw water in by contraction. Cures gulma, spleen and abdominal disease and disorders of vāta, pitta and kapha; **jala-basti** brings clarity of the dhātus, senses and antaḥkaraṇa, glow and a kindled fire (2.26–29).

**HP neti**: a smooth thread of **one span (vitasti)** passed through the nose and out of the mouth; it cleans the skull, gives divine sight and destroys the diseases above the shoulders (2.29–30). **HP nauli**: shoulders bent, the belly turned right and left with speed like a whirlpool; it kindles the fire and is the **crown of haṭha practices** (2.33–34).
**Gajakaraṇī** (HP 2.38) is described after the six as a form of dhauti: bring the contents of the stomach up to the throat by moving apāna, like an elephant.

**GS antar-dhauti**: **vātasāra** — draw air in through the beak-shaped mouth (kākī), churn the belly, expel through the anus; destroys all diseases and increases the gastric fire. **Vārisāra** — drink water to the throat and pass it out through the anus; makes the body **divine (deva-deha)**. **Vahnisāra/agnisāra** — press the navel to the spine **100 times**; destroys abdominal disease. **Bahiṣkṛta** — fill the stomach with air by kākī-mudrā, hold for **half a yāma (≈1½ hours)**, then wash the śakti-nāḍī standing navel-deep in water (prakṣālana).

**GS danta-dhauti (5)**: danta-mūla — rub the teeth with **khadira (catechu) juice** or clean earth; **jihvā-śodhana** — the index, middle and ring fingers rub the tongue root, then the tongue is rubbed with butter and drawn out with iron tongs (it lengthens the tongue, aiding khecarī); **karṇa-randhra (two ears)** — index and ring finger, bringing the inner nāda; **kapāla-randhra** — rub the hollow above the forehead with the right thumb; cures kapha disorders and gives divine sight.

**GS hṛd-dhauti (3)**: **daṇḍa** — a stalk of **plantain, turmeric or cane** pushed into the oesophagus and drawn out; removes heart disease, kapha and pitta. **Vamana** — drink water to the throat, look up, vomit it; cures kapha and pitta. **Vāsa (vastra)** — swallow a fine cloth **four fingers wide** and draw it out; cures gulma, fever, spleen disorders and leprosy (skin disease). **Mūla-śodhana**: clean the rectum with a **turmeric root or the middle finger**; removes constipation and indigestion.

**GS vasti (2)**: **jala-vasti** — navel-deep in water in utkaṭāsana, contract and dilate the anus; cures prameha, udāvarta and krūra-vāyu and gives a body like Kāmadeva. **Śuṣka (sthala) vasti** — in paścimottānāsana, move the intestines down and contract and dilate the anus by **aśvinī-mudrā**; it ends constipation and increases the gastric fire.

**GS neti** (thread through the nose and out of the mouth) gives **khecarī-siddhi**, destroys kapha disorders and gives divine sight. **Laulikī**: swing the belly forcefully from side to side; destroys all disease and kindles the fire. **GS trāṭaka** gives **śāmbhavī** and divine sight. **GS kapālabhāti (3)**: **vātakrama** (breath), **vyutkrama** (water drawn through the nose and expelled from the mouth), **śītkrama** (water sucked in through the mouth, expelled through the nose); all destroy kapha disorders.
**Divine sight (divya-dṛṣṭi) in GS** comes from **kapāla-randhra dhauti, neti and trāṭaka**. Karṇa-randhra (ear) dhauti gives nāda, not divine sight.
traps: **Nauli vs laulikī**: HP calls it nauli; GS calls the same belly churning **laulikī**. GS has no nauli, and HP has no laulikī.
**Kapāla-randhra** is a kind of **danta-dhauti**, not antar-dhauti. **Bahiṣkṛta**, despite the name ('external'), is an **antar-dhauti**. **Daṇḍa, vamana and vāsa** are the three **hṛd-dhautis**.
**Vārisāra** makes the body divine; **vātasāra** destroys all diseases; **vahnisāra** is the one with **100** strokes of the navel. Don't swap these.

**Secret like a golden box** = trāṭaka (HP). **Bellows of a blacksmith** = kapālabhāti in HP, but bhastrikā prāṇāyāma is also compared to bellows (HP 2.59–64). A question about the six karmas means kapālabhāti.
**Gajakaraṇī is not one of the six karmas** in HP. It is mentioned after them as a kind of dhauti. The Haṭharatnāvalī's eight karmas (aṣṭakarma) do include it.
**GS kapālabhāti** is mostly done with water through the nose and mouth (vyutkrama, śītkrama), unlike HP's rapid breathing.

facts: Vibhūti Pāda (55 sūtras) opens with **dhāraṇā** (3.1: fixing the mind on one place), **dhyāna** (3.2: unbroken flow of cognition) and **samādhi** (3.3: only the object shines). The three together on one object are **saṃyama** (3.4); they are *antaraṅga* compared with the first five limbs (3.7) but *bahiraṅga* to nirbīja samādhi (3.8).
Three **pariṇāmas** of citta: **nirodha** (3.9), **samādhi** (3.11) and **ekāgratā** (3.12); and of the elements: **dharma, lakṣaṇa, avasthā** (3.13).

Selected siddhis: kūrma-nāḍī → steadiness (3.31); light in the head → vision of siddhas (3.32); navel cakra → knowledge of the body's arrangement (3.29); throat pit → end of hunger and thirst (3.30); moon → arrangement of stars (3.27); pole star → their motion (3.28); heart → knowledge of citta (3.34).
Knowledge of puruṣa (3.35) brings **prātibha, śrāvaṇa, vedana, ādarśa, āsvāda, vārtā** (3.36) — obstacles to samādhi though powers in the waking state (3.37).

Mastery of **udāna** → not touching water, mud, thorns, and rising (3.39); of **samāna** → radiance (3.40). Mastery of the elements → the eight siddhis beginning with **aṇimā** and **kāya-sampat** (3.45), which is *rūpa, lāvaṇya, bala, vajra-saṃhananatva* (3.46).
Discrimination between sattva and puruṣa brings omnipotence and omniscience (3.49); non-attachment even to that leads to **kaivalya** (3.50). Do not be proud when invited by the celestials (3.51).

**Nirodha-pariṇāma** (3.9): the saṃskāras of outgoing activity (vyutthāna) are suppressed and those of restraint (nirodha) appear. Its flow becomes calm through saṃskāra (3.10). **Samādhi-pariṇāma** (3.11): scattering (sarvārthatā) declines and one-pointedness rises. **Ekāgratā-pariṇāma** (3.12): the subsiding and the arising idea are alike.

Saṃyama on the **three pariṇāmas → knowledge of past and future** (3.16). On word, meaning and idea → understanding the cries of all beings (3.17). On **saṃskāras → knowledge of previous births** (3.18). On another's idea (pratyaya) → knowledge of their mind (3.19).

On the form of the body → **invisibility** (3.21). On karma, fast or slow → knowledge of the **time of death** and ariṣṭas, portents (3.22). On friendliness and the other bhāvanās → those strengths (3.23). On strength → the **strength of an elephant** (3.24). On the inner light → knowledge of the subtle, hidden and distant (3.25). On the **sun → knowledge of the worlds** (bhuvana-jñāna, 3.26).

**Prātibha** (intuition) gives everything (3.33). Loosening the cause of bondage → **entering another body** (3.38). The relation of **ear and ākāśa → divine hearing** (3.41). Body and ākāśa → **lightness like cotton, moving through space** (3.42). **Mahāvideha** destroys the veil over the light (3.43).

**Bhūta-jaya** (3.44): saṃyama on the five aspects of the elements — gross (sthūla), essential form (svarūpa), subtle (sūkṣma), connection (anvaya) and purpose (arthavattva). **Indriya-jaya** (3.47): on grasping (grahaṇa), svarūpa, asmitā, anvaya, arthavattva. From it come speed like the mind, action without the body and mastery of pradhāna (3.48).
**Eight siddhis (aṣṭa-siddhi)**: aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, garimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, vaśitva.

Saṃyama on **the moment (kṣaṇa) and its sequence** → knowledge born of discrimination (**vivekaja-jñāna**, 3.52), which is **tāraka** (liberating), covers all objects at all times, and is without sequence (3.54). When sattva and puruṣa are equally pure, there is **kaivalya** (3.55).
**Numbering**: Vyāsa's text has 55 sūtras in this pāda. Some editions split or merge a sūtra, so numbers can be off by one; match the content, not only the number.
traps: **Sun → worlds, moon → arrangement of the stars, pole star (dhruva) → their movement.** These three are often swapped.
**Navel → body's arrangement; throat-pit → end of hunger and thirst; kūrma-nāḍī → steadiness; light at the crown → seeing siddhas; heart → knowledge of citta.**
**Udāna mastery → not touching water, mud and thorns, and rising (utkrānti). Samāna mastery → radiance (jvalana).** Don't swap prāṇa names.
The **powers of 3.36** (prātibha, śrāvaṇa, vedana, ādarśa, āsvāda, vārtā) are **obstacles to samādhi** (3.37), although they count as powers in the waking state.
**Pariṇāmas of the citta** are nirodha, samādhi and ekāgratā. **Pariṇāmas of the elements and senses** are dharma, lakṣaṇa and avasthā. Mixed lists are a common trick.

facts: **195 sūtras in four pādas**: Samādhi (51), Sādhana (55), Vibhūti (55), Kaivalya (34). Vyāsa's *bhāṣya* is the oldest commentary; others: Vācaspati Miśra (Tattva-vaiśāradī), Bhoja (Rāja-mārtaṇḍa), Vijñānabhikṣu (Yoga-vārttika).
Key definitions: ***atha yogānuśāsanam*** (1.1); ***yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ*** (1.2); ***tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam*** (1.3); ***abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyāṃ tan-nirodhaḥ*** (1.12).

Where things are: vṛttis 1.5–11; Īśvara 1.23–29; antarāyas 1.30–32; bhāvanās 1.33; kriyā yoga 2.1; kleśas 2.3–9; heya–hetu–hāna–upāya 2.16–26; eight limbs 2.29; yamas 2.30–31; niyamas 2.32; āsana 2.46–48; prāṇāyāma 2.49–53; pratyāhāra 2.54–55; dhāraṇā 3.1; saṃyama 3.4; pariṇāmas 3.9–13; sources of siddhis 4.1; dharmamegha 4.29; kaivalya 4.34.
Sequence questions are common: arrange topics in the order they appear (e.g. citta-vṛtti → Īśvara → kleśas → dhāraṇā → citta-pariṇāma).

**Vṛttis (1.5–11)**: five, kliṣṭa or akliṣṭa — pramāṇa, viparyaya, vikalpa, nidrā, smṛti. **Viparyaya** is false knowledge (1.8); **vikalpa** is a verbal idea without an object (1.9); **nidrā** is a vṛtti resting on absence (1.10).

**Means of nirodha**: abhyāsa and vairāgya (1.12–16); **īśvara-praṇidhāna** (1.23); **citta-prasādana** by maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā (1.33); and the alternatives of 1.34–39 (prāṇa expulsion, sense-object engagement, *viśokā jyotiṣmatī*, *vīta-rāga* minds, dream and sleep knowledge, *yathābhimata-dhyāna*).

**Samādhi types**: samprajñāta with **vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, asmitā** (1.17); asamprajñāta (1.18); **bhava-pratyaya** for videhas and prakṛti-layas (1.19); **upāya-pratyaya** with **śraddhā, vīrya, smṛti, samādhi, prajñā** (1.20); savitarka, nirvitarka, savicāra, nirvicāra samāpattis (1.42–44); **ṛtambharā prajñā** (1.48); nirbīja (1.51).

**Sādhana Pāda**: kriyā-yoga = **tapas, svādhyāya, īśvara-praṇidhāna** (2.1); five kleśas (2.3); four states of kleśas — **prasupta, tanu, vicchinna, udāra** (2.4); dṛśya made of the guṇas, existing for **bhoga and apavarga** (2.18); seven-fold prajñā (2.27); **pratipakṣa-bhāvanā** against vitarkas (2.33–34).

**Āsana** = *sthira-sukham āsanam* (2.46); by loosening effort and samāpatti with the infinite (2.47); then **no assault by the pairs of opposites** (2.48). **Prāṇāyāma** = *śvāsa-praśvāsayor gati-vicchedaḥ* (2.49); bāhya, ābhyantara, stambha, observed by **deśa, kāla, saṅkhyā**, long and subtle (2.50); the **fourth** goes beyond the external and internal (2.51).

**Kaivalya Pāda**: siddhis from **janma, oṣadhi, mantra, tapas, samādhi** (4.1); **nirmāṇa-citta** from asmitā alone (4.4); karma of the yogin is **neither white nor black**, of others threefold (4.7); **dharmamegha samādhi** (4.29); kaivalya — the guṇas return to their source, or the power of consciousness rests in itself (4.34).

**Commentaries in order**: Vyāsa (Bhāṣya, c. 4th–5th c.); Vācaspati Miśra (Tattvavaiśāradī, 9th–10th c.); Bhoja (Rājamārtaṇḍa, 11th c.); Vijñānabhikṣu (Yogavārttika, 16th c.); Nāgojī Bhaṭṭa; Hariharānanda Āraṇya (Bhāsvatī, 20th c.).
traps: **Kriyā-yoga's three** (tapas, svādhyāya, īśvara-praṇidhāna) are also the **last three niyamas**. A question on kriyā-yoga will not include śauca or santoṣa.
**Upāya-pratyaya's five** (śraddhā, vīrya, smṛti, samādhi, prajñā) are the same as the Buddhist five strengths (bala/indriya). Don't confuse them with the four bhāvanās of 1.33.
**Kleśa states**: prasupta, tanu, vicchinna, udāra. **Citta-bhūmis**: kṣipta, mūḍha, vikṣipta, ekāgra, niruddha. These two lists of names are often mixed.
Count: **Samādhi 51, Sādhana 55, Vibhūti 55, Kaivalya 34 = 195**. Some editions count 196 because they split or merge one sūtra.

facts: **Nine antarāyas** (YS 1.30): *vyādhi* (disease), *styāna* (dullness), *saṃśaya* (doubt), *pramāda* (carelessness), *ālasya* (laziness), *avirati* (sensual craving), *bhrānti-darśana* (false perception), *alabdha-bhūmikatva* (not reaching a stage), *anavasthitatva* (instability).
**Five companions** (*vikṣepa-sahabhuvaḥ*, YS 1.31): *duḥkha, daurmanasya, aṅgamejayatva, śvāsa, praśvāsa*.
Remedy: **eka-tattva-abhyāsa** (1.32); also through Īśvara-praṇidhāna, the antarāyas disappear and inner consciousness is gained (1.29).
The **four bhāvanās** (1.33): *maitrī* towards the happy, *karuṇā* towards the suffering, *muditā* towards the virtuous, *upekṣā* towards the wicked → *citta-prasādana*.

Haṭha Pradīpikā's version: six that destroy yoga (1.15: atyāhāra, prayāsa, prajalpa, niyamāgraha, jana-saṅga, laulya) and six that bring success (1.16: utsāha, sāhasa, dhairya, tattva-jñāna, niścaya, jana-saṅga-parityāga).

**Īśvara (1.24–28)**: a special puruṣa untouched by **kleśa, karma, vipāka and āśaya** (1.24); in him is the unsurpassed seed of omniscience (1.25); he is the teacher of the ancients, not limited by time (1.26); his word is **praṇava (Om)** (1.27); its **japa and contemplation of its meaning** (1.28) lead to **inner awareness and the disappearance of the obstacles** (1.29).

**Meanings**: *styāna* — mental dullness or unwillingness; *pramāda* — not cultivating the means of samādhi; *ālasya* — heaviness of body and mind; *avirati* — craving for sense objects; *alabdha-bhūmikatva* — not reaching a stage; *anavasthitatva* — not holding a stage once reached.

**Companions**: *duḥkha* — pain (ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika); *daurmanasya* — despair when a wish is blocked; *aṅgamejayatva* — **trembling of the limbs**; *śvāsa* — unwanted inhalation; *praśvāsa* — unwanted exhalation.

**1.34–39, other ways to steady the mind**: expelling and holding the breath (1.34); sense-perception of subtle objects (1.35); the sorrowless, luminous state (1.36); a mind fixed on one free of attachment (1.37); knowledge from dreams and sleep (1.38); meditation on anything one likes (1.39). Mastery extends **from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude** (1.40).
traps: **9 antarāyas vs 5 companions** (*sahabhuvaḥ*). 'Śvāsa–praśvāsa' are companions, not obstacles. 'Saṃśaya' is an obstacle, not a companion.
**Maitrī → happy, karuṇā → suffering, muditā → virtuous, upekṣā → wicked.** Matching questions shuffle the pairs.
**Ālasya** (sloth, a heaviness of body) vs **styāna** (the mind's unwillingness) vs **pramāda** (carelessness about the means).

facts: **Five kleśas** (YS 2.3): *avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa, abhiniveśa*. Avidyā is the field of the others (2.4).
**Four states** of kleśas (2.4): *prasupta* (dormant), *tanu* (thin), *vicchinna* (interrupted), *udāra* (active).

Definitions: avidyā — taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self (2.5); asmitā — identifying seer with seeing (2.6); rāga follows pleasure (2.7); dveṣa follows pain (2.8); abhiniveśa — clinging to life, present even in the wise (2.9).

Removal: subtle kleśas by returning to their source (*pratiprasava*, 2.10); their active modifications by **dhyāna** (2.11). **Kriyā yoga** (tapas, svādhyāya, Īśvara-praṇidhāna) is practised to weaken them and to cultivate samādhi (2.1–2).
Kleśas are the root of the *karmāśaya* (2.12), which ripens as birth, life-span and experience (*jāti, āyu, bhoga*, 2.13).
**2.8**: dveṣa follows pain. **2.9**: **abhiniveśa** (clinging to life) flows by its own nature and is **found even in the learned**. **2.14**: the fruits are joy or sorrow, from merit or demerit.
**2.15**: to the discriminating, all is suffering because of **pariṇāma** (change), **tāpa** (anxiety), **saṃskāra** (impressions) and the **conflict of the guṇa-vṛttis**.
**Sāṃkhya names for the five kleśas** (the five viparyayas, Vyāsa on 2.3): avidyā = **tamas**, asmitā = **moha**, rāga = **mahāmoha**, dveṣa = **tāmisra**, abhiniveśa = **andha-tāmisra**.
traps: **Avidyā has four forms** (2.5): taking the impermanent as permanent, the impure as pure, the painful as pleasant, and the non-self as self.
**Dhyāna removes the gross kleśa-vṛttis** (2.11); the **subtle kleśas** are removed by **pratiprasava**, dissolving them back into their cause (2.10).
**Asmitā** in 2.6 is a kleśa: identifying the seer with the instrument of seeing. It is not the same as the 'asmitā' stage of samprajñāta samādhi (1.17).

facts: **Five paṭalas**: (1) philosophy — views of the schools, Vedānta; (2) the body as microcosm — nāḍīs, fire, the jīva; (3) prāṇa, practice, the **four stages** (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti), four āsanas (siddha, padma, ugra/paścimottāna, svastika); (4) **ten mudrās**; (5) obstacles, four kinds of yoga, cakras, rāja yoga.
Nāḍīs: 3,50,000 in the body; **14 important**; 3 chief — iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā; inside suṣumnā is **citrā**.
Four kinds of yoga (5.9): **mantra, haṭha, laya, rāja**. Four kinds of aspirant: **mṛdu, madhya, adhimātra, adhimātratama**, attaining success in 12, 6, 3 years and fastest respectively (5.10–17).
Ten mudrās (4): mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, jālandhara, mūlabandha, viparītakaraṇī, uḍḍīyāna, vajrolī, śakticālana.
Up-prāṇas and their functions: nāga — belching; kūrma — opening the eyes; kṛkara — hunger/sneezing; devadatta — yawning; dhanañjaya — pervades, does not leave even the corpse.
**Aspirant → yoga** (ch. 5): **mṛdu** suits **mantra yoga**, **madhya** suits **laya yoga**, **adhimātra** suits **haṭha yoga**, and **adhimātratama** is fit for all four.
**Āsanas**: Śiva Saṃhitā mentions 84 but describes only **four** — **siddha, padma, ugra (paścimottāna), svastika**. **Pratīkopāsanā** (gazing at one's own shadow) is described in chapter 5.
**Obstacles to yoga** (ch. 5) are grouped under **bhoga** (enjoyment), **dharma** (ritual religion) and **jñāna** (wrong knowledge).
traps: **Nāḍī count**: Śiva Saṃhitā gives **3,50,000** nāḍīs (14 important); HP and most other texts give **72,000**.
**Four kinds of yoga** (mantra, haṭha, laya, rāja) is Śiva Saṃhitā's list. The **Yoga-tattva Upaniṣad** has the same four.

facts: Common classes: **meditative** (padma, siddha, svastika, sukha, vajra), **relaxative** (śava, makara, bālāsana), **cultural/corrective** (all others: forward bends, backward bends, twists, inversions, balances).
By position: standing, sitting, prone (bhujaṅga, śalabha, dhanura, makara), supine (śava, uttānapāda, sarvāṅga, hala, matsya).
Backward bends: bhujaṅga, śalabha, dhanura, uṣṭra, cakra, matsya. Forward bends: paścimottāna, pādahasta, hala. Balances: vṛkṣa, garuḍa, natarāja, bakāsana, kukkuṭa.

Effects asked: sarvāṅgāsana and matsyāsana (as its counter-pose) — thyroid; halāsana's counter-pose — cakrāsana/matsyāsana; maṇḍūkāsana, ardha-matsyendrāsana — pancreas and diabetes; śavāsana — relaxation, hypertension.
Patañjali's definition: ***sthira-sukham āsanam*** (YS 2.46), mastered by relaxing effort and meditating on the infinite (2.47); result: freedom from the pairs of opposites (2.48).

**Inversions**: śīrṣa, sarvāṅga, viparīta-karaṇī, hala. **Twists**: ardha-matsyendra, vakra, marīcy. **Counter-pose rule**: follow a forward bend with a backward bend; matsyāsana follows sarvāṅgāsana and halāsana.
traps: **Makarāsana is relaxative** (prone). **Śavāsana is the supine relaxative.** Neither is meditative.
**Vajrāsana** can be done just after meals (it aids digestion). Most other āsanas need an empty stomach.

facts: **Mitāhāra**: pleasant, sweet food, offered to Śiva, leaving **one quarter** of the stomach empty (Haṭha Pradīpikā 1.58). Gheraṇḍa (5.22): half the stomach food, a quarter water, a quarter left for air.

**Pathya (HP 1.62–63)**: good grains (wheat, rice, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice), milk, ghee, brown sugar, butter, honey, dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), cucumber/patola, **five greens** (jīvantī, vāstuka, mūlya/akṣī, meghanāda, punarnavā), mung and pure water.

**Apathya (HP 1.59–61)**: bitter, sour, pungent, salty, hot; green vegetables (in general), sour gruel, oil, **sesame**, mustard, alcohol, fish, meat, curd, buttermilk, horse gram (*kulattha*), jujube, oil-cake, asafoetida, garlic; reheated or stale food.

**Gheraṇḍa (5.17–31)** lists pathya (rice, barley, wheat, mung, māṣa, caṇaka, patola, jackfruit, etc.) and forbidden items in order — curd, horse gram, wood-apple (*kapittha*), citron (*jambīra*), onion and so on — in the third (Mitāhāra) section of chapter 5.
Things to avoid at the start of practice (HP 1.61): fire, women, travel; at the start, early-morning bathing and fasting are forbidden.
**Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā mouthful measure**: **8** for a renunciant (muni), **16** for a forest-dweller, **32** for a householder.
**HP 1.64–66**: young, old, very old, sick or weak — **all succeed through practice**. Success does not come from wearing the yogi's dress or talking about yoga; practice alone is the cause.
traps: **Empty space**: HP mitāhāra leaves **¼** of the stomach empty; GS gives **½ food, ¼ water, ¼ air**; Caraka leaves **⅓** empty.
**Milk, ghee, wheat, rice, barley, mung, honey and dry ginger are pathya**. **Curd, buttermilk, sesame, mustard, horse gram (kulattha), alcohol, fish and meat are apathya.** Curd is the classic trap.
**Fasting and early-morning cold baths are forbidden at the start** of practice (HP 1.61), along with fire, women and travel.

facts: **Haṭha Pradīpikā: 15 āsanas** — svastika, gomukha, vīra, kūrma, kukkuṭa, uttāna-kūrma, dhanura, matsyendra, paścimottāna, mayūra, śava, siddha, padma, siṃha, bhadra. 84 are taught by Śiva; the best four: siddha, padma, siṃha, bhadra; and siddhāsana is the best of all (1.35–43).
**Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā: 32 āsanas** out of 84 lakh / 84 taught by Śiva (2.1–6), including bhujaṅga, śalabha, makara, uṣṭra, vṛṣa, garuḍa, gorakṣa, saṅkaṭa, maṇḍūka, uttāna-maṇḍūka, vṛkṣa, yoga, śava.

Typical facts asked: gomukha — right ankle beside the left buttock (HP 1.20); mayūra — destroys gulma, dropsy, spleen diseases (HP 1.31); paścimottāna — makes the breath flow in the back channel, kindles the gastric fire (HP 1.29); bhujaṅga — toes to navel on the ground (GS 2.42).
**Śiva Saṃhitā** describes four: siddha, padma, ugra (paścimottāna), svastika.

**HP order of the 15**: svastika, gomukha, vīra, kūrma, kukkuṭa, uttāna-kūrma, dhanura, matsyendra, paścimottāna, mayūra, śava, siddha, padma, siṃha, bhadra. **The first is svastikāsana**. Āsana gives **sthairya (steadiness), ārogya (health) and aṅga-lāghava (lightness of body)** (1.17).

**HP svastikāsana**: both soles between the thighs and calves, body straight (*jānūrvor antare samyak kṛtvā pāda-tale ubhe*). **Gomukha**: **right ankle beside the left buttock**, left ankle beside the right, like a cow's face. **Vīra**: one foot on the opposite thigh, the other thigh on the other foot. **Kūrma**: press the anus with the crossed ankles (*gudaṃ nirudhya gulphābhyāṃ vyutkrameṇa*).

**HP kukkuṭa**: from padmāsana, pass the hands between the thighs and calves and rise on the palms. **Uttāna-kūrma**: from kukkuṭa, hold the neck with the hands and lie on the back like a tortoise. **Dhanura**: hold the toes and draw them to the ears like a bow.

**HP matsyendrāsana** kindles the gastric fire and is a **weapon that destroys all diseases**; daily practice awakens kuṇḍalinī and makes **the moon (candra) steady** (1.26–27). **Paścimottāna** makes the breath flow through suṣumṇā, kindles the fire, slims the belly and gives health (1.28–29); HP calls it the foremost āsana (*āsanāgryam*).

**HP mayūra**: balance on the palms with the elbows at the navel and the body straight like a stick. It destroys **gulma, dropsy (jalodara) and spleen disease**, and digests even poison (*kālakūṭa*) (1.30–31). **Śava**: lying on the back like a corpse; removes fatigue and rests the mind (*śrama-haraṃ citta-viśrānti-kārakam*, 1.32).

**HP siddhāsana** (1.35–43): heel pressed at the perineum, the other above the genitals, chin on the chest, gaze between the eyebrows. It is the best of all āsanas, purifies the **72,000 nāḍīs**, and once it is mastered **the three bandhas come by themselves**. It is also called vajra, mukta and gupta. **Padmāsana**: right foot on the left thigh, left foot on the right (*vāmorūpari dakṣiṇaṃ ca caraṇaṃ*); in the baddha form the hands cross behind the back to hold the big toes.

**HP siṃhāsana**: mouth wide open, jālandhara, gaze at the nose-tip (*vyātta-vaktro jalandhreṇa nāsāgram avalokayet*); it holds the three bandhas together. **Bhadrāsana**: ankles under the scrotum on either side of the perineum, feet held with the hands; it destroys all diseases and is also called **gorakṣāsana**.

**GS 32**: siddha, padma, bhadra, mukta, vajra, svastika, siṃha, gomukha, vīra, dhanura, mṛta (śava), gupta, matsya, matsyendra, gorakṣa, paścimottāna, utkaṭa, saṅkaṭa, mayūra, kukkuṭa, kūrma, uttāna-kūrma, uttāna-maṇḍūka, maṇḍūka, vṛkṣa, garuḍa, vṛṣa, śalabha, makara, uṣṭra, bhujaṅga, yoga. The **last five are śalabha, makara, uṣṭra, bhujaṅga, yoga**.

**GS descriptions often asked**: **matsya** — lie on the back from mukta-padmāsana, head held by the elbows; **vajra** — thighs firm like a vajra, feet beside the anus; **vīra** — one foot on the other thigh, the other foot turned back; **gupta** — feet hidden between the knees and thighs, sit on the feet; **svastika** — feet held between the thighs and calves, body straight; **utkaṭa** — on the toes, heels raised, anus on the heels.

**More from GS**: **vṛṣa** — right heel under the anus, left leg turned back on the ground; **vṛkṣa** — stand on the left leg with the right foot at the root of the left thigh; **śalabha** — prone, hands under the chest, legs raised one span; **makara** — prone, chest on the ground, legs stretched, head held in the arms; it **increases the bodily fire**; **uttāna-maṇḍūka** — from maṇḍūka, head held by the elbows; **bhujaṅga** — body from the toes to the navel on the ground, it **awakens Bhujaṅgī-devī (kuṇḍalinī)** and increases the fire.
traps: **HP lists 15, GS 32**. Both say Śiva taught 84 (GS: 84 lakh, of which 84 are best and 32 useful for people). **Śiva Saṃhitā has 4**: siddha, padma, ugra (= paścimottāna) and svastika.
**Svastika vs gupta vs siddha**: in svastika the feet are tucked between thighs and calves. In gupta they are hidden and you sit on them. In siddha a heel presses the perineum.
**First āsana in HP = svastika**, but the **best (four)** are siddha, padma, siṃha, bhadra, and the **single best is siddha**.
**Kūrma vs uttāna-kūrma**: in kūrma the crossed ankles press the anus. Uttāna-kūrma is kukkuṭa turned onto the back.
**Matsyendra makes the moon steady and awakens kuṇḍalinī** (HP). **Bhujaṅga awakens kuṇḍalinī** (GS). The text named in the question decides which is correct.
**Āsanas in GS but not in HP** include bhujaṅga, śalabha, makara, uṣṭra, garuḍa, vṛkṣa, vṛṣa, maṇḍūka, utkaṭa, saṅkaṭa, matsya, gupta and mukta.

facts: **Eight kumbhakas** (HP 2.44): sūrya-bhedana, ujjāyī, sītkārī, śītalī, bhastrikā, bhrāmarī, mūrcchā, plāvinī. **Sahita** and **kevala** (2.71–74) are the two kinds of retention, not among the eight.

Effects: sūrya-bhedana — purifies the skull, destroys vāta disorders and worms (2.50); **ujjāyī** — removes kapha in the throat, kindles the gastric fire (2.53); sītkārī — beauty, no hunger, thirst or sleep (2.55); śītalī — cures gulma, spleen, fever, pitta, and poison (2.58); bhastrikā — pierces the three granthis (2.67).

Why prāṇāyāma: when the breath moves the mind moves (2.2); nāḍīs full of impurities block the breath from the central channel, so purify them first (2.4–6). Nāḍī-śodhana: inhale left, exhale right, and so on, four times a day, up to 80 rounds (2.7–11).
Three stages of prāṇāyāma: sweating (lowest), trembling (middle), the breath reaching the head (highest) (2.12).

**2.1**: once āsana is steady, the yogin with a moderate diet should practise prāṇāyāma as the guru teaches. **2.3**: as long as the breath stays in the body, life remains; death is its departure. **2.15**: prāṇa is tamed slowly, **as lions, elephants and tigers are tamed**; otherwise it kills the practitioner.

**2.16–17**: correct prāṇāyāma destroys all diseases; wrong practice causes them — **hiccup, asthma, cough, and pain in the head, ears and eyes**. **2.13**: rub the sweat produced into the body to make it firm and light. **2.14**: at the start, a diet of **milk and ghee** is recommended.

**Nāḍī-śodhana** (2.7–10): inhale through the left (candra), hold, exhale through the right; inhale right, hold, exhale left. **2.11**: kumbhaka **four times a day** — morning, noon, evening, midnight — slowly increased to **80** rounds. The nāḍīs are purified in **three months** (2.10).
**Signs of purified nāḍīs** (2.19–20): a lean body, glow, hearing of nāda, clear eyes, freedom from disease, control of bindu, a kindled fire.

**Kevala kumbhaka** (2.72–74): when retention happens without inhalation or exhalation, **kevala** is attained, and nothing in the three worlds is out of reach. Until then it is sahita. **2.76**: there is no rāja yoga without haṭha and no haṭha without rāja; practise both until success.
**Signs of success in haṭha** (2.78): slimness, a bright face, clear nāda, clear eyes, health, control of bindu, a kindled fire and purified nāḍīs.
traps: **Grades of prāṇāyāma** (2.12): lowest — **sweat**; middle — **trembling**; highest — **steadiness** (the breath reaches the head). Options sometimes reverse the order.
**Nāḍī-śodhana begins with the left nostril** (candra/iḍā), while sūrya-bhedana begins with the right.
Prāṇāyāma is to be done **four times a day, up to 80 kumbhakas** per sitting. Numbers like 20 or 108 are distractors.

facts: Part of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; three vallīs: **Śikṣā Vallī**, **Brahmānanda (Ānanda) Vallī**, **Bhṛgu Vallī**.
**Pañca-kośa** (Brahmānanda Vallī 2.1–5): annamaya, prāṇamaya, manomaya, vijñānamaya, ānandamaya.
Brahman is ***satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma*** (2.1). Creation order (2.1): from the Self, space → air → fire → water → earth → plants → food → person.
Śikṣā Vallī: the convocation address — ***satyaṃ vada, dharmaṃ cara, svādhyāyān mā pramadaḥ***; ***mātṛdevo bhava, pitṛdevo bhava, ācāryadevo bhava, atithidevo bhava*** (1.11).
Bhṛgu Vallī: Bhṛgu learns from Varuṇa through tapas that Brahman is food, prāṇa, mind, understanding and finally **bliss** (3.1–6).
**Size**: Śikṣā Vallī 12 anuvākas, Brahmānanda Vallī 9, Bhṛgu Vallī 10. It opens with the peace chant ***śaṃ no mitraḥ śaṃ varuṇaḥ***. *Saha nāv avatu* is its chant too, shared with the Kaṭha.

**Śikṣā (phonetics) has six elements** (1.2): **varṇa** (letter), **svara** (accent), **mātrā** (length), **bala** (effort), **sāma** (evenness), **santāna** (continuity). The **five great combinations (mahāsaṃhitā)** (1.3): of the worlds, lights, knowledge, offspring and the self. The vyāhṛtis bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ and the fourth, **mahaḥ**, come in 1.5.

**Ānanda Vallī**: ***yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha*** (2.4, 2.9); ***raso vai saḥ*** (2.7); one who thinks Brahman does not exist becomes non-existent (2.6). **Ānanda-mīmāṃsā** (2.8): bliss rising **a hundredfold** at each step, from the human to Brahmā.

**Bhṛgu Vallī**: Brahman is that from which beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return (*yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante*, 3.1). Food precepts: **do not despise food** (3.7), do not reject food (3.8), **make much food** (3.9), turn no one away from your house (3.10).

**Śikṣā Vallī, more**: 1.3 the five great combinations (*mahā-saṃhitā*) — on the worlds, the lights, knowledge, progeny and the self; 1.5 the vyāhṛtis *bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ* and the fourth, ***mahaḥ***, made known by **Māhācamasya**; 1.6 the Person in the space of the heart, and the way out through the palate to the crown; 1.9 every virtue is to go together with **svādhyāya and pravacana** (study and teaching) — Nāka Maudgalya says these two alone, 'for that is tapas'; 1.10 Triśaṅku's song of realisation; 1.11 *mātṛ-devo bhava, pitṛ-devo bhava, ācārya-devo bhava, atithi-devo bhava*; give with faith, with modesty, with awe and with understanding.

**Ānanda and Bhṛgu Vallīs, more**: 2.6 *so'kāmayata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya* — He desired 'may I be many', performed tapas, created all this and entered it; 2.8 *bhīṣāsmād vātaḥ pavate* — from fear of Him the wind blows and the sun rises; the **ānanda-mīmāṃsā** then measures bliss, each step a hundred times the last, from the joy of a strong young man up to the bliss of Brahman; 3.7–10 four vows about food — *annaṃ na nindyāt* (do not despise food), *annaṃ na paricakṣīta* (do not reject it), *annaṃ bahu kurvīta* (make food plentiful), and turn no guest away; the knower sings *aham annam, aham annādaḥ* — 'I am food, I am the eater of food.'
traps: **Kośa order**: anna → prāṇa → mano → **vijñāna** → ānanda. Mano and vijñāna are the pair most often swapped.
**Creation order** (2.1): ākāśa → vāyu → **agni** → āpaḥ → pṛthvī. Fire comes before water.
**Bhṛgu's teacher is his father, Varuṇa**, and the method is **tapas**. Don't confuse him with Uddālaka teaching Śvetaketu (Chāndogya).
**The fourth vyāhṛti is *mahaḥ*** (Taittirīya 1.5), taught by Māhācamasya: *mahaḥ* is Brahman, the Self, and the other three are its limbs.

facts: Attributed to **Gorakṣanātha**; six upadeśas. Chapter 1 — origin of the body and the five nija-śaktis of Śiva: icchā, kriyā, māyā, prakṛti, vāk, each with five qualities.

Chapter 2 — **nine cakras** (ādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, kaṇṭha, tālu, bhrū, nirvāṇa, ākāśa), **16 ādhāras**, **3 lakṣyas**, **5 vyomas**; and an **eight-limbed yoga** in which yama is mastery of senses, food, sleep, cold, wind and heat.

Chapter 3 — the body as cosmos (*piṇḍa-brahmāṇḍa*): continents, oceans, mountains and castes inside the body (e.g. skin = Krauñca-dvīpa, urine = salt ocean, forehead = Śrīśaila, right conduct = brāhmaṇa).
Later chapters: knowledge of the piṇḍa, samarasa (union), and the avadhūta yogi.

**Six upadeśas**: 1 **piṇḍotpatti** (origin of the body), 2 **piṇḍa-vicāra** (examining the body: cakras, ādhāras, lakṣyas, vyomas), 3 **piṇḍa-saṃvitti** (the body as cosmos), 4 **piṇḍādhāra** (the support of the body, śakti), 5 **piṇḍa-pada-samarasa-karaṇa** (union, with the **sadguru**), 6 **avadhūta-yogi-lakṣaṇa**. Sadguru is discussed in **chapter 5**.

**Three lakṣyas**: **antar** (inner), **bahir** (outer) and **madhya** (middle). **Five vyomas (vyoma-pañcaka)**: ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, tattvākāśa, sūryākāśa. Of the haṭha texts, SSP is the one that describes the vyoma-pañcaka.

**SSP's eight limbs**: **yama** — conquest of all the senses and of food, sleep, cold, wind and heat (so mastery of the senses, food and sleep comes from yama, not pratyāhāra); **niyama** — control of the mind's activity, solitude, non-attachment, indifference, contentment with what comes, dispassion and devotion to the guru's feet.

**Āsana in SSP: three** — svastika, padma, siddha. **Prāṇāyāma: four** — **recaka, pūraka, kumbhaka, saṅghaṭṭīkaraṇa**. **Pratyāhāra**: withdrawing the mind from the flow of the guṇas. **Dhāraṇā**: holding the inner self steady. **Dhyāna**: contemplating the Self in all beings. **Samādhi**: equanimity in all states.

**Nine cakras in ascending order**: brahma/ādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, nābhi (maṇipūra), hṛdaya (anāhata), kaṇṭha (viśuddha), tālu, bhrū (ājñā), nirvāṇa (brahmarandhra), ākāśa. There are **16 ādhāras**, beginning with the big toe.
traps: **SSP has 3 āsanas** (svastika, padma, siddha). **Śiva Saṃhitā has 4** (siddha, padma, ugra, svastika). **Ugrāsana is not in SSP.**
**SSP prāṇāyāma = 4 kinds** (recaka, pūraka, kumbhaka, saṅghaṭṭīkaraṇa), not the 8 kumbhakas of HP or GS.
**Nine cakras** in SSP, not six. The extra ones are tālu, nirvāṇa and ākāśa.

facts: **Six āstika darśanas** and founders: Nyāya — Gautama; Vaiśeṣika — Kaṇāda; Sāṃkhya — Kapila; Yoga — Patañjali; Pūrva Mīmāṃsā — Jaimini; Uttara Mīmāṃsā/Vedānta — Bādarāyaṇa (Vyāsa).

**Sāṃkhya**: 25 tattvas — puruṣa, prakṛti, mahat (buddhi), ahaṃkāra, manas, 5 jñānendriyas, 5 karmendriyas, 5 tanmātras, 5 mahābhūtas. Prakṛti is the balance of **sattva, rajas, tamas**; the guṇas are not evolutes. Main text: Īśvarakṛṣṇa's **Sāṃkhya Kārikā** (72 verses) with Gauḍapāda's commentary.
Sāṃkhya accepts **three pramāṇas** (pratyakṣa, anumāna, śabda); its causation is **satkāryavāda** (effect pre-exists in the cause). It is non-theistic; Yoga adds Īśvara ("seśvara Sāṃkhya").
Nyāya accepts four pramāṇas (adds upamāna); Mīmāṃsā (Kumārila) six (adds arthāpatti, anupalabdhi).
*Dhyānaṃ nirviṣayaṃ manaḥ* is Sāṃkhya Sūtra 6.25.

**Basic texts**: Nyāya Sūtra (Gautama/Akṣapāda); Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (Kaṇāda/Ulūka); Sāṃkhya Kārikā (Īśvarakṛṣṇa; the lost Ṣaṣṭitantra is older, and the Sāṃkhya Sūtra is late); Yoga Sūtra (Patañjali); Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (Jaimini); Brahma Sūtra (Bādarāyaṇa). Pairs: Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya–Yoga, Mīmāṃsā–Vedānta.

**Sāṃkhya's four classes** (SK 3): **prakṛti only** (cause, not effect); **seven prakṛti-vikṛti** (mahat, ahaṃkāra, five tanmātras); **sixteen vikāra only** (manas, 10 indriyas, 5 mahābhūtas); **puruṣa — neither cause nor effect**.

**Five reasons for satkāryavāda** (SK 9): *asad-akaraṇāt, upādāna-grahaṇāt, sarva-sambhavābhāvāt, śaktasya śakya-karaṇāt, kāraṇa-bhāvāt*. **Five proofs of prakṛti** (SK 15) and **five proofs of puruṣa** (SK 17: *saṅghāta-parārthatvāt*… ). **Puruṣas are many** (SK 18).

**Three kinds of suffering** (SK 1): **ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika**. The puruṣa–prakṛti union is like the **lame man and the blind man** (SK 21); prakṛti withdraws like a **dancer** after showing herself (SK 59).
**Guṇas**: sattva — light (laghu), illuminating (prakāśaka); rajas — stimulating, mobile (cala); tamas — heavy (guru), enveloping (varaṇaka) (SK 13).
**Ahaṃkāra in three forms**: sāttvika (vaikārika) produces manas and the 10 indriyas; tāmasika (bhūtādi) produces the tanmātras; rajas (taijasa) helps both.
**Vedānta schools**: Advaita — Śaṅkara; Viśiṣṭādvaita — Rāmānuja; Dvaita — Madhva; Dvaitādvaita — Nimbārka; Śuddhādvaita — Vallabha; Acintya-bhedābheda — Caitanya.
**Causation**: Sāṃkhya – satkāryavāda (pariṇāma); Advaita – vivartavāda (apparent change); Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika – **asatkāryavāda/ārambhavāda**; Buddhists – pratītyasamutpāda.
**Pramāṇas**: Cārvāka 1 (pratyakṣa); Vaiśeṣika and Buddhists 2; Sāṃkhya and Yoga 3; Nyāya 4; Prabhākara Mīmāṃsā 5 (adds arthāpatti); Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and Advaita 6 (adds anupalabdhi).

**Nyāya** (Gautama; Nyāya Sūtra in 5 adhyāyas; bhāṣya by **Vātsyāyana**): liberation (*apavarga*) comes from true knowledge of **16 padārthas** (pramāṇa, prameya, saṃśaya … nigrahasthāna); four pramāṇas; God as the efficient cause; the five-membered syllogism. **Vaiśeṣika** (Kaṇāda; 10 adhyāyas; Praśastapāda's *Padārtha-dharma-saṅgraha*): **six padārthas** — dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, samavāya (abhāva was added later as the seventh); **nine dravyas** (earth, water, fire, air, ākāśa, time, space, self, mind); **atomism** (*paramāṇu-vāda*).

**Pūrva Mīmāṃsā** (Jaimini; 12 adhyāyas; **Śabara-bhāṣya**; schools of **Kumārila Bhaṭṭa** and **Prabhākara**): dharma is known from Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ*); the Veda is eternal and authorless; knowledge is self-valid (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*); ritual produces an unseen potency (*apūrva*). **Yoga darśana** accepts Sāṃkhya's 25 tattvas and adds **Īśvara**, a special puruṣa (26 in all).

**Sāṃkhya literature**: the Sāṃkhya Kārikā has **72 kārikās** (the Chinese version is called the 'Golden Seventy'); commentaries — Gauḍapāda-bhāṣya, **Vācaspati's Tattva-kaumudī**, Māṭhara-vṛtti, Yuktidīpikā; the later Sāṃkhya Sūtra has **Vijñānabhikṣu's Sāṃkhya-pravacana-bhāṣya**. Lineage: **Kapila → Āsuri → Pañcaśikha** (SK 70). The 'creation of the intellect' (*pratyaya-sarga*, SK 46–51) has **50 divisions**: 5 viparyaya (errors), 28 aśakti (incapacities), 9 tuṣṭi (complacencies) and 8 siddhi (attainments).

**Order of evolution in Sāṃkhya** (SK 22): prakṛti → **mahat** (buddhi) → **ahaṃkāra** → the group of sixteen (manas, five jñānendriyas, five karmendriyas, five tanmātras) → from the five tanmātras the **five mahābhūtas**. Buddhi has eight forms (SK 23): four sāttvika — dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, aiśvarya — and their four tāmasa opposites. The subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) of 18 (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, ten indriyas, five tanmātras) transmigrates (SK 40). Liberation is by **knowledge alone** (*jñānena cāpavargaḥ*, SK 44).
traps: **Yoga Sūtra 1.7**: the pramāṇas of Yoga are **pratyakṣa, anumāna, āgama** (= Sāṃkhya's three). Upamāna is Nyāya's fourth.
**Āstika vs nāstika**: Cārvāka, Jaina and Bauddha are nāstika (they reject Vedic authority). Sāṃkhya is āstika even though it does not accept God.
**Mahat is prakṛti-vikṛti** (both cause and effect), not pure prakṛti. **Manas is a vikṛti only.**
**Padārthas and tattvas**: Nyāya 16; Vaiśeṣika 6 (7 with abhāva); Sāṃkhya 25; Yoga 26.
**Bhāṣyas**: Nyāya — Vātsyāyana; Vaiśeṣika — Praśastapāda; Mīmāṃsā — Śabara; Yoga — Vyāsa; Sāṃkhya Kārikā — Gauḍapāda (and Vācaspati's Tattva-kaumudī); Brahma Sūtra — Śaṅkara and the other ācāryas.
**Pairs of darśanas** (*samāna-tantra*): Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika; Sāṃkhya–Yoga; Pūrva–Uttara Mīmāṃsā.
**Sūtra lengths**: Nyāya 5 adhyāyas; Vaiśeṣika 10; Mīmāṃsā 12; Brahma Sūtra 4; Yoga Sūtra 4 pādas; Sāṃkhya is read from the Kārikā (72 verses).

facts: **Tridoṣa**: vāta (air + space), pitta (fire + water), kapha (water + earth). Nānātmaja disorders (Caraka): vāta **80**, pitta **40**, kapha **20**.
**Six rasas** and doṣas: madhura, amla, lavaṇa calm vāta; madhura, tikta, kaṣāya calm pitta; kaṭu, tikta, kaṣāya calm kapha.
Seasonal cycle (*caya–prakopa–praśama*): vāta — summer, rains, autumn; pitta — rains, autumn, hemanta; kapha — śiśira, spring, summer.
**Triguṇa diet** (Gītā 17.8–10): sāttvika — juicy, oily, nourishing; rājasika — bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry; tāmasika — stale, tasteless, putrid, leftover.

**Doṣa qualities**: **vāta** — dry, light, cold, rough, subtle, mobile; **pitta** — slightly oily, sharp, hot, light, fleshy-smelling, flowing, liquid; **kapha** — heavy, cold, soft, oily, sweet, stable, slimy. Kapha gives **cohesion (saṃśleṣaṇa)**, pitta transformation, vāta movement.
**Seasonal cycle (caya → prakopa → praśama)**: **vāta** — grīṣma → varṣā → śarad; **pitta** — varṣā → śarad → hemanta; **kapha** — śiśira → vasanta → grīṣma.

**Diet by prakṛti**: vāta — warm, oily, heavy; sweet, sour, salty tastes. Avoid dry, cold, light food and pungent, bitter, astringent tastes. Pitta — cool; sweet, bitter, astringent. Kapha — light, dry, warm; **pungent, bitter, astringent**. **Dull (manda) and heavy (guru) food is forbidden for kapha**.

**Seven dhātus**: rasa, rakta, māṃsa, meda, asthi, majjā, śukra. **Three malas**: purīṣa, mūtra, sveda. **13 agnis**: 1 jāṭharāgni, 5 bhūtāgnis, 7 dhātvagnis. **Four states of agni**: sama (balanced), viṣama (vāta), tīkṣṇa (pitta), manda (kapha).

**Three pillars of life (trayopastambha)**: āhāra, nidrā, brahmacarya. **Caraka's eight factors of diet** (*aṣṭa āhāra-vidhi-viśeṣāyatana*): prakṛti (nature of the food), karaṇa (preparation), saṃyoga (combination), rāśi (quantity), deśa (place), kāla (time), upayoga-saṃsthā (rules of eating), upayoktā (the eater).

**Stomach division (Caraka)**: one part solid food, one part liquid, **one third left empty** for the doṣas. **Hita-bhuk, mita-bhuk, ṛta-bhuk** — eat what is wholesome, in measure and in season — is the classical rule. Many diseases today are blamed on an irregular routine.
traps: **Stomach space**: in Ayurveda (Caraka), **⅓** is left empty. In the haṭha texts (GS 5.22; HP *mitāhāra*), half is food, a quarter water and **¼ left for air**. Check which text the question names.
**Nānātmaja disorders**: vāta 80, **pitta 40**, kapha 20 (the order is the reverse of 20-40-80 in some options).
**Kapha = water + earth; pitta = fire + water; vāta = air + space.** Options often swap pitta's water for earth.

facts: Gharote and Ganguly (*Teaching Methods for Yogic Practices*) distinguish **instructional** methods for theory (lecture, discussion, question-answer) and methods for **practical skills** (demonstration, directed practice, part/whole method).
Principles of teaching: from **known to unknown**, **simple to complex**, whole–part–whole, progression, individual differences.
Practical lesson sequence: verbal introduction → demonstration → salient points → advantages/precautions → question-answer → students' practice and correction.
Types of questions in a lesson: introductory (arouse interest), comprehension (check understanding), thought-provoking (relate ideas), comparison (similarities/differences).
The teacher should demonstrate personally; instructions should be brief, slow, clear and repeated when needed.

**General methods**: lecture, demonstration, discussion, project, **inductive** (examples → rule) and **deductive** (rule → examples), whole method and part method. **Edgar Dale's cone of experience** puts **direct, purposeful experience** at the base (most concrete) and verbal symbols at the top.
traps: **Inductive = from particular to general** (examples first). **Deductive = from general to particular** (rule first).
**Maxims of teaching**: known → unknown, simple → complex, concrete → abstract, particular → general, whole → part, empirical → rational.

facts: Adult skeleton: **206 bones** (axial 80, appendicular 126). Longest — femur; smallest — stapes (ear).
Bone shapes: **long** (femur, humerus), **short** (carpals, tarsals), **flat** (skull vault, sternum, scapula, ribs), **irregular** (vertebrae), **sesamoid** (patella).

Joints: fibrous (immovable, e.g. skull sutures), cartilaginous (slightly movable, e.g. intervertebral discs), **synovial** (freely movable) — types: ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle, condylar.
Vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral (fused), 4 coccygeal (fused) — 33 in a child, 26 in an adult.
Muscle's functional unit is the **sarcomere**; movements at joints include flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, inversion, eversion, protraction, retraction.

**Skull 22 bones** (8 cranial, 14 facial); **ribs 12 pairs** — 7 true, 3 false, 2 floating. The **hyoid** is the only bone that articulates with no other bone. The **patella** is the largest sesamoid bone.

**Synovial joint types**: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip); hinge (elbow, knee); **pivot (atlas–axis, C1–C2)**; saddle (the thumb's carpometacarpal joint); gliding (between the carpals); condyloid (wrist). **Bone cells**: osteoblasts build bone, **osteoclasts resorb it**, osteocytes maintain it.
traps: **Osteoporosis** = loss of bone density. **Osteoarthritis** = wear of joint cartilage. **Rheumatoid arthritis** is autoimmune.
**Atlas (C1)** carries the skull ('yes' nodding); the **atlas pivots on the axis (C2)** ('no' rotation).

facts: A written lesson plan organises the teacher's thinking, builds confidence and is a record for future plans; it should be specific, detailed and allow for individual differences.
Parts of a lesson plan: general and specific objectives, materials, introduction, presentation (demonstration and instructions), practice, evaluation, recapitulation.
Class arrangement: clean, airy, quiet hall; students in staggered rows so all can see the teacher's demonstration; the teacher may use a raised platform for large groups.
**Herbart's five formal steps** of a lesson plan: **preparation → presentation → comparison/association → generalisation → application**, often followed by recapitulation.
traps: **Preparation comes before presentation**. In Herbart's steps, **generalisation comes before application**.

facts: YS 2.1: ***tapaḥ-svādhyāyeśvara-praṇidhānāni kriyā-yogaḥ*** — austerity, self-study and surrender to Īśvara.
Purpose (2.2): to cultivate samādhi and to weaken the kleśas (*kleśa-tanūkaraṇa*).
The same three are the last three niyamas (2.32). Fruits: tapas → perfection of body and senses (2.43); svādhyāya → union with the chosen deity (2.44); Īśvara-praṇidhāna → samādhi (2.45).

**Vyāsa on 2.1**: yoga does not succeed without **tapas**, but tapas should **not disturb the body** and should keep the mind clear. **Svādhyāya** = japa of purifying mantras such as praṇava, or study of texts on liberation. **Īśvara-praṇidhāna** = offering all actions to the supreme teacher and giving up their fruits.
traps: **Patañjali's kriyā-yoga (2.1)** ≠ **Lahiri Mahāśaya's Kriyā Yoga** (Babaji → Lahiri → Yukteśvar → Yogānanda) ≠ the **ṣaṭkarma 'kriyās'** of haṭha.
Kriyā-yoga's purpose (2.2) is **samādhi-bhāvana and kleśa-tanūkaraṇa**: it thins the kleśas, it does not destroy them.

facts: **Yamas** (YS 2.30): ahiṃsā, satya, asteya, brahmacarya, aparigraha — universal, called **mahāvrata** (2.31).
**Niyamas** (2.32): śauca, santoṣa, tapas, svādhyāya, Īśvara-praṇidhāna. Against contrary thoughts, cultivate the opposite (*pratipakṣa-bhāvana*, 2.33–34).

Siddhis (2.35–45): ahiṃsā → hostility abandoned nearby; satya → actions bear fruit; asteya → all jewels; brahmacarya → vigour; aparigraha → knowledge of past births; śauca → disgust for one's body, purity of sattva; santoṣa → unsurpassed happiness; tapas → perfection of body and senses; svādhyāya → union with the deity; Īśvara-praṇidhāna → samādhi.
**Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā** and the Haṭha texts list **ten yamas and ten niyamas**; there śauca is a yama, and dāna, āstikya, Īśvara-pūjana, siddhānta-śravaṇa, hrī, mati, japa, vrata are niyamas.

**Full siddhi list**: ahiṃsā → those near give up hostility (2.35); satya → actions bear the promised fruit (2.36); asteya → all jewels appear (2.37); brahmacarya → **vīrya (vigour)** (2.38); aparigraha → **knowledge of the how of past births** (2.39); śauca → disgust for one's own body and non-contact with others (2.40), then purity of sattva, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses and fitness for self-vision (2.41).

**Niyama results**: santoṣa → **unsurpassed happiness** (2.42); tapas → perfection of body and senses through the destruction of impurity (2.43); svādhyāya → **union with one's chosen deity** (iṣṭa-devatā, 2.44); īśvara-praṇidhāna → **perfection of samādhi** (2.45).

**Vitarkas** (2.34): violence etc. done, caused to be done or approved (kṛta, kārita, anumodita); arising from **greed, anger, delusion**; mild, medium or intense. Vyāsa multiplies them to **81** kinds. Their fruit is endless pain and ignorance, so cultivate the opposite.
**Mahāvrata** (2.31): the yamas are universal — not limited by **birth (jāti), place (deśa), time (kāla) or circumstance (samaya)**.
traps: **Aparigraha → past births**, not wealth. **Asteya → jewels.** These two are commonly swapped.
**Svādhyāya → iṣṭa-devatā**; **īśvara-praṇidhāna → samādhi**. Both relate to God, so they are easy to mix up.
**Śauca has two results**: outer (disgust for one's own body) in 2.40 and inner (sattva-śuddhi …) in 2.41.

facts: YS 2.49: prāṇāyāma is breaking the flow of inhalation and exhalation, after āsana is mastered.

Three kinds (2.50): **bāhya** (external), **ābhyantara** (internal), **stambha** (sudden suspension), regulated by place, time and number, becoming long and subtle; a **fourth** goes beyond external and internal (2.51).
Results: the covering over the light dwindles (2.52) and the mind becomes fit for **dhāraṇā** (2.53).
**Vyāsa on 2.52** quotes: *tapo na paraṃ prāṇāyāmāt* — there is no austerity higher than prāṇāyāma; from it comes purification and the light of knowledge.
**YS 1.34**: *pracchardana-vidhāraṇābhyāṃ vā prāṇasya* — the mind is also steadied by **expelling and holding the breath**. This is the first mention of breath in the sūtras.
traps: **Stambha-vṛtti** (2.50) is a **sudden suspension**. The **fourth (caturtha)** prāṇāyāma (2.51) goes **beyond both external and internal**, and is often compared with kevala kumbhaka.
Prāṇāyāma comes **after āsana is perfected** (*tasmin sati*, 2.49). **Deśa, kāla, saṅkhyā** = place, time, number.

facts: **Ten mudrās** (HP 3.6–7): mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, uḍḍīyāna, mūla, jālandhara, viparītakaraṇī, vajrolī, śakticālana.

Mahāmudrā: left heel at the perineum, right leg stretched, hold the toes, jālandhara (3.10–11); cures consumption, leprosy, constipation, gulma, indigestion (3.17). Mahāvedha removes wrinkles, grey hair and trembling (3.29); viparītakaraṇī likewise after six months (3.81).
Khecarī: tongue turned back into the cavity above the palate; "eating cow's flesh and drinking the immortal liquor" are coded terms for it (3.47–49).
**Three bandhas**: mūla (perineum), uḍḍīyāna (abdomen), jālandhara (throat).

**Purpose**: kuṇḍalinī, the support of all yoga, sleeps blocking the mouth of suṣumṇā; the mudrās awaken it so prāṇa enters suṣumṇā (3.1–5). The ten mudrās **destroy old age and death** and give the eight siddhis, and are to be kept secret (3.8–9).

**Mahāmudrā**: practise first on the left side and then the right, the same number of times (3.15). **Mahābandha**: left heel at the perineum, right foot on the left thigh, jālandhara, then mūla; it unites the three nāḍīs at the eyebrow centre (3.19–22). **Mahāvedha**: from mahābandha, palms on the ground, gently strike the buttocks on the ground; prāṇa leaves iḍā and piṅgalā and enters the middle (3.26–28). The three are done **eight times a day, every three hours**.

**Khecarī**: lengthen the tongue until it touches the eyebrow centre by cutting the frenum **a hair's breadth every seven days** for **six months**, with a sharp clean blade like a snuhī leaf, and by milking it (3.32–36). The practitioner is free of disease, death, sleep, hunger, thirst and fainting, and is unaffected by karma and time (3.38–41).

**Uḍḍīyāna**: pull the abdomen above and below the navel back towards the spine; it is the lion that kills the elephant of death, and even an old man becomes young by practising it for **six months** (3.55–60). **Mūla-bandha**: press the perineum with the heel and contract the anus, drawing **apāna upward** (3.61); prāṇa and apāna, and nāda and bindu, unite; urine and faeces lessen and the old become young (3.64–65).

**Jālandhara**: contract the throat and press the chin firmly on the chest; it binds the network of nāḍīs and stops the nectar falling from the sky (moon) into the fire (3.70–71). It cures throat diseases, and by contracting the throat iḍā and piṅgalā are held (3.72–73). **Sequence in prāṇāyāma**: jālandhara at the end of inhalation, uḍḍīyāna at the end of retention.

**Viparītakaraṇī**: the **sun at the navel** swallows the nectar flowing from the **moon at the palate**; invert them, navel up, head down (3.77–79). Increase the time a little each day; after **six months** wrinkles and grey hair disappear, and practice of **one yāma (three hours)** daily conquers death (3.81–82).

**Vajrolī** (3.83–99) with its two forms **sahajolī** and **amarolī**. **Śakticālana** (3.104–123): kuṇḍalinī, coiled like a serpent and also called **kuṭilāṅgī, bhujaṅgī, śakti, īśvarī, arundhatī**, is stirred by holding the kanda and doing **bhastrikā**, for an hour and a half morning and evening. The **kanda** lies 12 aṅgulas above the anus, four fingers wide, as if wrapped in a white cloth (3.113).
traps: **HP has 10 mudrās; GS has 25**. Among the GS 25 are aśvinī, pāśinī, kākī, mātaṅginī, bhujaṅginī, śāmbhavī, the five dhāraṇās, yoni and tāḍāgī; these are not in HP's list.
**Mūla draws apāna upward; jālandhara blocks the nectar at the throat; uḍḍīyāna draws prāṇa up into suṣumṇā.** Matching questions pair each bandha with its effect.
**'Eating cow's flesh'** = turning the tongue back into the palate (go = tongue), and **'drinking the immortal liquor'** = the nectar. It is code for khecarī, not literal.
**Sun = navel, moon = palate** in viparītakaraṇī. Don't reverse them.

facts: Birth years (often asked as sequences): Lahiri Mahāśaya 1828; Rāmakṛṣṇa 1836; Dayānanda Sarasvatī 1824; Vivekānanda 1863; Śrī Aurobindo 1872; Śivānanda (Rishikesh) 1887; T. Krishnamacharya 1888; Paramahaṃsa Yogānanda 1893; Mahesh Yogi 1918; B.K.S. Iyengar 1918; Svāmī Rāma 1925.

Institutions: **Kaivalyadhama**, Lonavla — Svāmī Kuvalayānanda (1924); **The Yoga Institute**, Santacruz — Śrī Yogendra (1918); **Bihar School of Yoga**, Munger — Svāmī Satyānanda (1964); **Divine Life Society** — Śivānanda (1936); **S-VYASA**, Bengaluru — H.R. Nagendra; **Patañjali Yogpeeth** — Svāmī Rāmdev; **MDNIY**, New Delhi.
Dayānanda founded the **Ārya Samāj** (1875); Vivekānanda the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) and wrote *Rāja Yoga* (1896); Aurobindo taught Integral Yoga.

**More birth years**: Ramaṇa Maharṣi 1879; Kuvalayānanda **1883**; Śivānanda **1887**; T. Krishnamacharya **1888**; Yogendra **1897**; Yogānanda 1893; Pattabhi Jois 1915; **B. K. S. Iyengar 1918**; Satyānanda **1923**; Dhīrendra Brahmacārī 1924; H. R. Nagendra 1943.

**Founding dates**: The Yoga Institute, Mumbai **1918** (oldest organised yoga centre); Self-Realization Fellowship (Yogānanda) **1920**; Kaivalyadhama **1924**, with the journal **Yoga Mīmāṃsā** the same year; Divine Life Society, Rishikesh **1936**; Bihar School of Yoga, Munger **1963–64**; Vivekananda Kendra 1972; **S-VYASA**, Bengaluru (Nagendra) 1986; Patanjali Yogpeeth (Ramdev) 2006.

**Key books**: Vivekānanda — *Rāja Yoga* (1896); Krishnamacharya — *Yoga Makaranda* (1934); Yogānanda — *Autobiography of a Yogi* (1946); Iyengar — *Light on Yoga* (1966); Satyānanda — *Āsana Prāṇāyāma Mudrā Bandha* (1969). Krishnamacharya taught Iyengar, Pattabhi Jois (Aṣṭāṅga Vinyāsa), Indra Devi and T. K. V. Desikachar (Viniyoga).

**Svāmī Vivekānanda** (12 Jan 1863, Kolkata – 4 July 1902, Belur): born **Narendranāth Datta**; guru **Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa** (met at Dakṣiṇeśvar, 1881). Spoke at the **Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 11 Sept 1893**; founded the **Vedanta Society** of New York (1894), the **Ramakrishna Mission** (1 May 1897) and **Belur Maṭh**. Taught four yogas as equal paths — *Karma Yoga*, *Bhakti Yoga*, *Rāja Yoga* (1896, with a translation of the Yoga Sūtra) and *Jñāna Yoga* — and 'practical Vedānta': serving people as worship of God. His birthday is **National Youth Day**.

**Śrī Aurobindo** (15 Aug 1872, Kolkata – 5 Dec 1950, Puducherry): educated in England; Baroda service; nationalist leader. The yogī **Viṣṇu Bhāskar Lele** taught him to silence the mind (1908), and in **Alipore jail (1908–09)** he saw Nārāyaṇa in everything. Came to **Pondicherry on 4 April 1910**. **Integral (Pūrṇa) Yoga**: not escape from life but its transformation — 'All life is yoga'; aspiration, rejection and surrender; the triple transformation (**psychic, spiritual, supramental**) and the descent of the **Supermind**. His collaborator was **Mirra Alfassa, 'the Mother'** (1878–1973); the Ashram dates from **24 Nov 1926**, and the Mother founded **Auroville** in 1968. Works: *The Life Divine*, *The Synthesis of Yoga*, *Essays on the Gita*, *The Secret of the Veda*, the epic *Savitri*; the journal *Arya* (1914–21).

**Ramaṇa Maharṣi** (30 Dec 1879, Tiruchuli – 14 April 1950, Tiruvannamalai): born **Veṅkaṭarāman**; a death-experience at **16 (Madurai, 1896)** left him established in the Self; he reached **Aruṇācala on 1 Sept 1896** and never left. He had no human guru and spoke of Aruṇācala as his guru. He was named 'Bhagavān Śrī Ramaṇa Maharṣi' by **Kāvyakaṇṭha Gaṇapati Muni** (1907). Method: **self-enquiry** (*ātma-vicāra*, 'Who am I?'), silence, or surrender. Works: *Nāṉ Yār?* (Who am I?), **Upadeśa Sāram** (30 verses), *Uḷḷadu Nāṟpadu* (Forty Verses on Reality), *Akṣaramaṇamālai*. Paul Brunton's *A Search in Secret India* (1934) made him known in the West.

**Maharṣi Dayānanda Sarasvatī** (12 Feb 1824, Ṭaṅkārā, Gujarat – 30 Oct 1883, Ajmer): born **Mūlaśaṅkar**; a Śivarātri vigil shook his faith in image worship and he left home; took saṃnyāsa from **Pūrṇānanda Sarasvatī**; studied grammar and the Veda under the blind guru **Svāmī Virajānanda** of Mathura. Founded the **Ārya Samāj at Bombay on 10 April 1875** (its ten principles were settled at Lahore in 1877). Call: 'Back to the Vedas'; against idolatry, caste by birth and child marriage; began *śuddhi*. Works: **Satyārtha Prakāśa** (1875), *Ṛgvedādi-bhāṣya-bhūmikā*, *Saṃskāra-vidhi*, and Hindi commentaries on the Veda. He practised yoga for years and taught aṣṭāṅga yoga and prāṇāyāma as part of the daily *sandhyā*.

**Śyāmācaraṇ Lāhiṛī (Lahiri Mahāśaya)** (30 Sept 1828, Ghurni, Nadia – 26 Sept 1895, Varanasi): a householder and government accountant; initiated into **Kriyā Yoga** by **Mahāvatār Bābājī** near **Ranikhet in 1861**; he revived Kriyā Yoga and gave it to householders of every caste and faith, and is called *Yogāvatār*. Disciples: **Śrī Yukteśvar Giri** (the guru of Paramahaṃsa Yogānanda), Pañcānan Bhaṭṭācārya and Bhūpendranāth Sānyāl. Yogānanda's *Autobiography of a Yogi* (1946) carried his teaching to the world.

**T. Krishnamacharya** (18 Nov 1888, Muchukundapura, Karnataka – 28 Feb 1989, Chennai): a scholar of the six darśanas and Āyurveda; by his own account he studied yoga for seven and a half years with **Rāmamohana Brahmacārī** near Lake Mānasarovar; from 1933 he taught at the **Mysore palace yogaśālā** under Kṛṣṇarāja Woḍeyar IV. Called the 'father of modern yoga': he linked āsana with the breath (*vinyāsa*) and fitted practice to the person (*viniyoga*) and to therapy. Works: **Yoga Makaranda** (1934), *Yogāsanagaḷu* (1941), *Yoga Rahasya* (ascribed to Nāthamuni), *Yogavallī*. Students: **B. K. S. Iyengar**, **K. Pattabhi Jois**, **Indra Devi**, his son **T. K. V. Desikachar** (Krishnamacharya Yoga Mandiram, Chennai, 1976) and A. G. Mohan.

**Svāmī Śivānanda Sarasvatī** (8 Sept 1887, Pattamadai, Tamil Nadu – 14 July 1963, Rishikesh): born **Kuppusvāmī**; a doctor who served in **Malaya**; took saṃnyāsa at Rishikesh in **1924** from **Svāmī Viśvānanda Sarasvatī**. Founded the **Divine Life Society (1936)** and the Yoga-Vedanta Forest Academy (1948). Taught the **Yoga of Synthesis** — 'Serve, Love, Give, Purify, Meditate, Realise' — and wrote about 300 books. Disciples: Cidānanda, Kṛṣṇānanda, **Satyānanda** (Bihar School of Yoga), **Viṣṇudevānanda** (Sivananda Yoga Vedanta Centres), Cinmayānanda (Chinmaya Mission), Satcidānanda (Integral Yoga) and Veṅkaṭeśānanda.

**Svāmī Rāma of the Himalayas** (1925, Garhwal – 13 Nov 1996): born **Brij Kiśor Dhasmānā**; brought up by his master **Baṅgālī Bābā** in the Himalayan cave tradition; by his own account he was Śaṅkarācārya of Karvīrpīṭham (1949–52) before returning to his master. At the **Menninger Foundation, Topeka (1970–71)** he showed voluntary control of heart rate, skin temperature and brain waves, including conscious deep sleep (yoga nidrā) — a landmark for biofeedback research. Founded the **Himalayan International Institute of Yoga Science and Philosophy** (1971; now at Honesdale, Pennsylvania) and the **Himalayan Institute Hospital Trust**, Dehradun (1989). Books: **Living with the Himalayan Masters** (1978), *Science of Breath*, *Yoga and Psychotherapy*, *Path of Fire and Light*, *Meditation and Its Practice*.

**Maharṣi Maheś Yogī** (12 Jan 1918 by most accounts, though the year is disputed – 5 Feb 2008, Vlodrop, Netherlands): born **Maheś Prasād Varmā** in central India; a physics graduate of Allahabad; disciple and secretary of **Svāmī Brahmānanda Sarasvatī ('Guru Dev')**, Śaṅkarācārya of Jyotirmaṭh. He began teaching in 1955 and founded the **Spiritual Regeneration Movement at Madras in 1958**. Taught **Transcendental Meditation (TM)** — twenty minutes twice a day with a mantra, without effort — and later the **TM-Sidhi programme** (1976). The Beatles stayed at his Rishikesh ashram in 1968. Books: **Science of Being and Art of Living** (1963) and a commentary on Gītā chapters 1–6 (1967). He also founded Maharishi International University (Iowa) and Maharishi Āyur-Veda.

**Paṇḍit Śrīrām Śarmā Ācārya** (20 Sept 1911, Āṃvalkheḍā, Agra – 2 June 1990, Haridwar, on Gāyatrī Jayantī): received the Gāyatrī mantra from **Madan Mohan Mālavīya**; guided from 1926 by his Himalayan guru **Svāmī Sarveśvarānanda**; completed **24 Gāyatrī mahāpuraścaraṇas** (24 lakh japa each, over 24 years); took part in the freedom movement. Founded the monthly **Akhaṇḍ Jyoti** (late 1930s), **Gāyatrī Tapobhūmi, Mathura (1953)**, the **Yug Nirmāṇ Yojanā**, **Śāntikuñj, Haridwar (1971)** and the **Brahmavarcas** research institute (1979): together the **All World Gayatri Pariwar**, led after him by his wife **Mātā Bhagavatī Devī Śarmā**. He wrote some 3,000 books and booklets and put the four Vedas, **108 Upaniṣads**, the six darśanas and the 18 Purāṇas into Hindi. Message: 'scientific spirituality', and *ham badleṅge, yug badlegā* ('we will change, the age will change').
traps: **Oldest institute = The Yoga Institute (Yogendra, 1918)**; **first scientific research = Kaivalyadhama (Kuvalayānanda, 1924)**.
**Dayānanda (1824) is older than Lahiri Mahāśaya (1828)**, and **Śivānanda (1887) is older than Krishnamacharya (1888)**. Close birth years are a common sequence trap.

**Gurus**: Vivekānanda — Rāmakṛṣṇa; Dayānanda — Virajānanda; Lahiri Mahāśaya — Mahāvatār Bābājī; Śivānanda — Viśvānanda Sarasvatī; Krishnamacharya — Rāmamohana Brahmacārī; Svāmī Rāma — Baṅgālī Bābā; Maheś Yogī — Brahmānanda Sarasvatī; Śrīrām Śarmā — Sarveśvarānanda; Yogānanda — Yukteśvar; Ramaṇa — no human guru.

**Systems**: Aurobindo — Integral (Pūrṇa) Yoga; Ramaṇa — ātma-vicāra; Lahiri Mahāśaya — Kriyā Yoga; Maheś Yogī — Transcendental Meditation; Śivānanda — Yoga of Synthesis; Krishnamacharya — vinyāsa and viniyoga; Śrīrām Śarmā — Gāyatrī sādhanā.

**Signature books**: *Satyārtha Prakāśa* — Dayānanda; *The Life Divine*, *The Synthesis of Yoga*, *Savitri* — Aurobindo; *Upadeśa Sāram* — Ramaṇa; *Yoga Makaranda* — Krishnamacharya; *Living with the Himalayan Masters* — Svāmī Rāma; *Science of Being and Art of Living* — Maheś Yogī; *Autobiography of a Yogi* — Yogānanda.

**Death years**: Dayānanda 1883; Lahiri Mahāśaya 1895; Vivekānanda 1902; Aurobindo and Ramaṇa both **1950**; Śivānanda 1963; Krishnamacharya 1989 (aged 100); Śrīrām Śarmā 1990; Svāmī Rāma 1996; Maheś Yogī 2008.
**Places**: Aurobindo — Puducherry; Ramaṇa — Tiruvannamalai (Aruṇācala); Śivānanda — Rishikesh; Śrīrām Śarmā — Śāntikuñj, Haridwar; Lahiri Mahāśaya — Varanasi; Krishnamacharya — Mysore, then Chennai.

facts: Dialogue between **Vasiṣṭha and Rāma**, about 32,000 verses in six prakaraṇas: Vairāgya, Mumukṣu, Utpatti, Sthiti, Upaśama, Nirvāṇa.
**Seven bhūmikās of knowledge**: śubhecchā, vicāraṇā, tanumānasā, sattvāpatti, asaṃsakti, padārthābhāvanī, turyagā.
Four gatekeepers of mokṣa: **śama, vicāra, santoṣa, sādhu-saṅga**.
Means to conquer the mind: company of the wise, giving up vāsanās, knowledge of the Self, stilling prāṇa (prāṇa-spanda-nirodha).
Also called **Mahā-Rāmāyaṇa, Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa, Ārṣa-Rāmāyaṇa**. It is attributed to **Vālmīki**, and the abridged **Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha** was made by Gauḍa Abhinanda (~6,000 verses).

**Definition**: *manaḥ-praśamanopāyo yoga ity abhidhīyate* — yoga is the means of calming the mind. **The two seeds of the citta**: **prāṇa-spanda** (movement of prāṇa) and **vāsanā**; when one is stilled, both are stilled.

**Ādhi and vyādhi**: ādhi (mental disturbance) gives rise to vyādhi (physical disease). Diseases are **ādhija**, born of the mind — **sāmānya** (ordinary, curable by usual means) and **sāra** (essential: rebirth, cured only by self-knowledge) — or **anādhija**, physical. This is the classic yogic account of **psychosomatic disease**.
There are also **seven stages of ignorance (ajñāna-bhūmikā)**, alongside the seven stages of knowledge.
traps: **Prakaraṇa order**: Vairāgya → Mumukṣu-vyavahāra → Utpatti → Sthiti → Upaśama → Nirvāṇa. Utpatti (creation) comes before Sthiti (existence).
**Four gatekeepers** (śama, vicāra, santoṣa, sādhu-saṅga) ≠ **Vedānta's sādhana-catuṣṭaya** (viveka, vairāgya, ṣaṭ-sampatti, mumukṣutva).
**First jñāna-bhūmikā = śubhecchā**, and **the seventh = turyagā**. Sattvāpatti is the fourth.

facts: Part of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; story of **Naciketā and Yama**, who grants three boons.
*Śreyas* (the good) vs *preyas* (the pleasant) (1.2.1–2); the Self is not born and does not die (1.2.18); ***nāyam ātmā pravacanena labhyo na medhayā na bahunā śrutena*** (1.2.23).
**Chariot image** (1.3.3–4): body — chariot, buddhi — charioteer, mind — reins, senses — horses, objects — roads, ātman — the lord of the chariot.
Hierarchy (1.3.10–11): objects > senses, mind > objects, buddhi > mind, mahat > buddhi, avyakta > mahat, puruṣa > avyakta — nothing beyond puruṣa.
Yoga is defined as the firm holding of the senses (2.3.11): ***tāṃ yogam iti manyante sthirām indriya-dhāraṇām***. *Uttiṣṭhata jāgrata prāpya varān nibodhata* (1.3.14).
**Structure**: 2 adhyāyas × 3 vallīs = **6 vallīs**. Naciketā's father is **Vājaśravas** (Auddālaki Āruṇi). He gives away old, barren cows, and in anger says 'to Death I give you'.

**Three boons** for the **three nights** Naciketā waits without food at Yama's house: (1) his father's calm and welcome; (2) the knowledge of the heavenly fire, which Yama names **Nāciketa-agni** and adds a jewelled garland (sṛṅkā); (3) what happens after death, the secret of the Self.

**Images**: a path as hard to walk as the **razor's edge** (*kṣurasya dhārā niśitā duratyayā*, 1.3.14); the **thumb-sized puruṣa** (aṅguṣṭha-mātra) in the heart (2.1.12–13); the eternal **aśvattha tree, roots above** (2.3.1); **101 nāḍīs of the heart**, one rising to the crown, leading to immortality (2.3.16).

**2.3.10**: when the **five senses and the mind are still and the buddhi does not stir**, that is the highest state (*paramā gati*), and in 2.3.11 this firm holding of the senses is called yoga. **1.2.15** praises **Om** as the word all the Vedas proclaim.

**Outline in this edition**: Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, Kaṭha śākhā; 2 adhyāyas of 3 vallīs each (119 mantras). 1.1 the story and the three boons; 1.2–1.3 Yama on the Self and the Supreme; adhyāya 2 — the obstacles to reaching the Lord and their removal, His seat in the heart, His all-pervasiveness, the world as an aśvattha tree, yoga practice, faith and liberation.

**The third boon** (1.1.20): *yeyaṃ prete vicikitsā manuṣye, astīty eke nāyam astīti caike* — 'when a man dies some say he is, some say he is not: teach me this.' Yama tests him with sons, cattle, long life and pleasures; Naciketā answers *na vittena tarpaṇīyo manuṣyaḥ* — man is not satisfied by wealth (1.1.27). Then: **Om** is the word all the Vedas declare (1.2.15–17); the Self is *aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān*, smaller than the small and greater than the great (1.2.20); *nāyam ātmā pravacanena labhyo na medhayā na bahunā śrutena* — it is won only by the one it chooses (1.2.23).

**Yoga passages**: 1.3.13 — merge speech in the mind, the mind in the knowing self, that in the great self, and that in the peaceful Self (*yacched vāṅ manasī prājñaḥ*); 2.1.1 — the Self-existent pierced the senses outward (*parāñci khāni*), so man looks out, but the wise one seeking immortality turns the gaze inward (*āvṛtta-cakṣuḥ*); 2.1.12–13 and 2.3.17 — the Person the size of a thumb (*aṅguṣṭha-mātraḥ puruṣaḥ*) dwells in the heart like a smokeless flame, to be drawn out patiently like the pith from a reed; 2.2.1 — the body is a city of **eleven gates**; 2.3.1 — the eternal **aśvattha with its root above and branches below**; 2.3.16 — the heart has **101 nāḍīs**, one of which goes to the crown, and rising by it one reaches immortality; 2.3.18 — Naciketā gained this knowledge and 'the whole method of yoga' (*yoga-vidhiṃ ca kṛtsnam*).
traps: **Chariot simile roles**: buddhi = **charioteer**, manas = **reins**, indriyas = horses. Mind is not the charioteer.
**Śreyas vs preyas**: the wise choose **śreyas (the good)**, the fool **preyas (the pleasant)**.
The Gītā's verse on the self that is not born and does not die (2.20) **echoes Kaṭha 1.2.18**. Questions may ask which text has it first.
**Gates of the body**: Kaṭha 2.2.1 — **eleven**; Gītā 5.13 and Śvetāśvatara 3.18 — **nine**.
**101 nāḍīs** (*śataṃ caikā ca hṛdayasya nāḍyaḥ*): Kaṭha 2.3.16 and Chāndogya 8.6.6; the Praśna (3.6) also starts from 101.

facts: Lineage: **Ādinātha (Śiva) → Matsyendranātha → Gorakṣanātha**; nine Nāthas and 84 siddhas are named in different lists. Haṭha Pradīpikā 1.5–9 gives a roll of mahāsiddhas (Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Śābara, Ānandabhairava, Cauraṅgī, Mīna, Gorakṣa, Virūpākṣa, Bileśaya, Manthāna, Bhairava, Siddhi, Buddha, Kanthaḍi, Koraṇṭaka, Surānanda, Siddhapāda, Carpaṭi, Kānerī, Pūjyapāda, Nityanātha, Nirañjana, Kapālī, Bindunātha, Kākacaṇḍīśvara, Allāma, Prabhudeva, Ghoḍācolī, Ṭiṇṭiṇi, Bhānukī, Nāradeva, Khaṇḍa, Kāpālika).
Works attributed to Gorakṣa: **Siddha Siddhānta Paddhati, Gorakṣa Śataka/Saṃhitā, Amaraugha Prabodha, Yoga Bīja** (sometimes), *Gorakhbānī* in Hindi.
**Twelve panths** (*bārah panth*): Satyanāthī, Dharmanāthī, Rāmapanth, Naṭeśvarī, Kanhaḍ, Kapilānī, Vairāg, Mannāthī, Āīpanth, Pāgalpanth, Dhajpanth, Gaṅgānāthī.
Nāth marks: split ears with large earrings (*kānphaṭa*), the *siṅgī-nād* (horn whistle) and the avadhūta ideal; haṭha yoga as the Nāth discipline.
